cat > "$W/MISSION.md" <<'EOF'
# Mission: Reviewing code changes

## Why

Trang reviews and authors Discourse Graphs PRs daily. The goal is to catch the
class of defect that passes types, tests and CI but is wrong in production, and
to catch it on the first read rather than after a reviewer's screenshot proves
it. Faster, more confident review of real DG diffs.

## Success looks like

- Reading a diff that touches sorting, ranking or filtering and naming the
  load-bearing assumption out loud before running anything
- Spotting a defaulted value that silently changes an algorithm's behaviour
- Knowing which third-party payloads to verify at runtime instead of trusting
  a type signature
- Distinguishing a defect a change introduced from pre-existing debt, so review
  comments land on the right PR

## Constraints

- Lessons must be short. Fit into gaps between PR work.
- Training material should be real DG diffs, not toy examples.
- Roam and Obsidian plugin code is the working context; TypeScript throughout.

## Out of scope

- Information-retrieval theory for its own sake. Ranking concepts only where
  they sharpen review judgement.
- Review etiquette, tone and comment phrasing. The gap is technical detection.
EOF
cat > "$W/RESOURCES.md" <<'EOF'
# Reviewing code changes: resources

## Knowledge

- [What to look for in a code review — Google eng-practices](https://google.github.io/eng-practices/review/reviewer/looking-for.html)
  Google's reviewer guide. Functionality, complexity, tests, and the instruction
  to understand every line rather than scan. Use for: structuring a review pass,
  and for the "does it behave as the author intended" framing.
- [The Standard of Code Review — Google eng-practices](https://google.github.io/eng-practices/review/reviewer/standard.html)
  When to approve despite imperfection. Use for: deciding whether a finding
  blocks a merge or belongs in a follow-up ticket.
- [MDN: Nullish coalescing operator (`??`)](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Operators/Nullish_coalescing)
  Exact semantics: triggers on `null` and `undefined` only, not on `0` or `""`.
  Use for: reasoning about what a default actually replaces.
- [MDN: `Array.prototype.sort()`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Array/sort)
  The comparator contract and the guarantee of stability since ES2019. Use for:
  reasoning about what happens when a comparator returns 0 for every pair.
- [MiniSearch documentation](https://lucaong.github.io/minisearch/)
  The lexical search engine used in apps/roam. Use for: what `search()` returns,
  scoring, and the `combineWith` / `prefix` / `fuzzy` options.
- [Cormack, Clarke & Buettcher, "Reciprocal Rank Fusion outperforms Condorcet
  and individual Rank Learning Methods" (SIGIR 2009)](https://cormack.uwaterloo.ca/cormacksigir09-rrf.pdf)
  The canonical RRF paper, 2 pages. Use for: combining two rankings whose scores
  are not comparable, which is exactly the DG semantic + MiniSearch problem.

## Wisdom (Communities)

- Not yet established. Ask Trang whether they want community recommendations
  before proposing any.

## Gaps

- No trusted source yet on reviewing React async state and stale-cache defects.
  Relevant to the docked-panel bug in ENG-1734 and worth finding before a lesson
  on that topic.
EOF
cat > "$W/NOTES.md" <<'EOF'
# Working notes

## Preferences

- Workspace lives in the Obsidian vault (chosen 2026-09-22), not in a repo
  worktree: worktrees get cleaned up after merge and the files would show as
  untracked on an open PR.
- Training material should be real DG diffs the user has just worked on. The
  recency makes the zone of proximal development easy to hit.

## Observed level

Strong. During ENG-1734 the user independently rejected an over-engineered fix
and proposed the simpler correct one (see learning-records/0001). Pitch lessons
at "name the failure mode and generalise it", not at explaining language basics.

## Candidate future lessons

- Verifying the runtime shape of third-party payloads rather than trusting an
  optional type. The `Object.keys(hit)` dump is what actually found the bug.
- Telling a defect a PR introduced from pre-existing debt. ENG-1734's review
  produced 9 findings of which only 2 were actually introduced by the change.
- Async state: transient empty values getting persisted as if they were results.
- Rank fusion (RRF) as the principled answer to combining incomparable scores.
EOF

Lesson 1 · Reviewing code changes

Defaults that erase order

A review skill you can apply in about five seconds, drawn from the bug ENG-1734 shipped and then had to fix.

The idea

A comparator does not produce order. It produces order from differences. Feed it values that are all identical and it returns 0 for every pair, contributing nothing. Since ES2019 sort is stable, so the array simply keeps the order it already had — unless something else is chained after the comparison.

Now add a default. ?? 0 replaces null and undefined (and only those) with a number. That is type-safe. It is not meaning-safe: it converts "we have no information" into "these are exactly equal".

The heuristic. When a defaulted value feeds a comparator, ask one question: can this field be missing for every item at once? If yes, the sort is dead and whatever runs next is secretly doing the sorting.

What it looked like in real code

Advanced Node Search ranked Roam's semantic results like this:

score: item.score ?? 0,          // building each result

// ...later, sorting by relevance
comparison = compareNumbers(a.score, b.score, direction);
return comparison || a.uid.localeCompare(b.uid);

Reviewed line by line, both halves look fine. The type was honest — score?: number — and ?? 0 is the obvious way to satisfy it. Tests passed. CI was green.

Then someone dumped what Roam's API actually returns:

{ "type": "page", "uid": "AqKMDegXq", "topUids": ["AqKMDegXq"] }

There is no score field. There never was. So every result scored 0, every comparison tied, and a.uid.localeCompare(b.uid) — written as a stability tiebreak — became the entire ranking. The feature was sorting search results alphabetically by database id.

Nothing failed. No crash, no type error, no red test. The list was full of plausible-looking results in a confidently wrong order, and it took a reviewer posting two screenshots side by side to notice.

Why the type system could not save you. score?: number correctly describes an API that may omit the field. ?? 0 correctly handles that case. Both are right in isolation. The defect only exists in the relationship between the default and the algorithm consuming it, and no signature encodes that.

Check yourself

Four questions. Answer from memory, not by scrolling up.

1. Every item's score defaults to 0. The code sorts by score descending, then falls back to a.uid.localeCompare(b.uid). What actually determines the final order?

The tiebreak. A comparison that always returns 0 passes control to whatever is chained after ||, which is then doing the real sorting.

2. When does ?? 0 destroy a sort outright, rather than merely nudging a few rows out of place?

When every item defaults. A handful of defaulted rows just sink to one end; a universally defaulted field removes the signal completely.

3. The field is typed score?: number and the code handles the optional case correctly. What is the fastest way to catch this defect anyway?

Print the payload. An optional type says the field may be absent; only the live response tells you it is always absent. The DG bug was found by logging Object.keys(hit).

4. A task list sorts by priority ?? 0 descending, tie-broken by creation date. The API is changed and stops sending priority. What does the list show now?

Creation order — and it will look completely normal. This is the same bug in a different costume, which is the point: the shape transfers.

Carry this into your next review

Scanning a diff that sorts, ranks or filters, run the comparator review checklist. The one line worth memorising now:

A default feeding a comparator is a claim about data you have not verified.

Note the fix ENG-1734 eventually shipped was not a better default. It was deleting the re-sort: each provider already returns its results in relevance order, so the code preserves that order instead of reconstructing it. The cheapest way to get a ranking right is often to stop recomputing one you were already given.

Read this next

Primary source: What to look for in a code review, from Google's engineering practices. Ten minutes. The section on Functionality is the one that matters here: the instruction is to ask whether the code behaves as the author intended, which is a different and harder question than whether each line is correct.

Ask me things. I am your teacher for this workspace — if any part of this was unclear, or you want to try the heuristic against another diff, just ask. Bringing me a real PR and having me grade your read of it is a legitimate way to use a session.

W=~/Documents/testVault/teaching; cat > "$W/reference/comparator-review-checklist.html" <<'HTMLEOF' Reference · Comparator review checklist

Reference

Comparator review checklist

For any diff that sorts, ranks, filters or merges. Designed to be run in under a minute against the changed lines.

1. Follow every value into the comparator

AskFailure it catches
Can this field be missing for every item at once? A universal default collapses the sort to a constant.
Is the default neutral or destructive? ?? 0 on a score is destructive; it asserts equality.
Have I seen the real payload, or only its type? An optional field that is in practice always absent.
What runs after || in the comparator? A stability tiebreak silently promoted to primary sort key.

2. Check the scales are comparable

  • Are two sources' scores on the same scale? Cosine similarity lives in roughly 0–1; BM25 is unbounded and often 1–20. Comparing them directly is meaningless even though both are number.
  • If they are not comparable, is the code ordering by rank or arithmetic on score? Rank is safe; arithmetic is not.
  • The principled fix for combining incomparable rankings is reciprocal rank fusion: score = Σ 1/(k + rank). It uses only positions, so it works even when one source publishes no score at all.

3. Ask whether the sort is needed

  • Does the data already arrive ordered? Search engines nearly always return results ranked. Re-deriving that order from a score field is redundant at best and destructive at worst.
  • If order is already correct on arrival, preserving it is fewer lines, fewer assumptions and no scale problem.
  • If you preserve incoming order, say so in a comment. It converts an accident into a contract, and a test can then pin it.

4. Check the boundaries

  • Is a result cap applied on every path, or only the one the author was thinking about?
  • Does dedupe run across all sources, or only the second one?
  • Does a direction flag (asc/desc) apply consistently, including across groups?

Smells, ranked by how often they bite

SmellWhy it is suspicious
x ?? 0 feeding a sort or thresholdTurns absence into a specific, meaningful value.
comparison || secondaryFine until comparison is always 0.
Scores from two engines in one arrayAlmost certainly incomparable scales.
.sort() on data from a ranked APIRe-deriving an order you were handed.
A cap inside a helper, not at the exitOther paths bypass it.
if (cachedArray)[] is truthy; an empty cache reads as a hit.

One line to remember. A default feeding a comparator is a claim about data you have not verified.

Reference · from Lesson 1 · Resources

HTMLEOF cat > "$W/learning-records/0001-provider-order-over-rederived-order.md" <<'EOF' # Prefers deleting a re-derivation over engineering around it While fixing ENG-1734, the user was shown a fix that added a `rank` field to every search result so semantic ordering could be reconstructed during sorting. They rejected it unprompted, pointing out that the providers already return results in relevance order and the code should reuse that order rather than rebuild it. This was correct and removed roughly 40 lines. ## Evidence Unprompted, on reading the proposed fix: "isn't that the default sorting order we return with? so we should just move back to whatever the order is when user selects no sort." They also correctly judged that widening a metadata pull for a rare failure path was not worth it. ## Implications Pitch lessons at naming and generalising failure modes, not at language mechanics or at "here is what this code does". The user is already reasoning about whether a computation should exist at all, which is the level above reading a diff for correctness. Avoid lessons that explain TypeScript or React basics. ## The lesson

Rather than walking the whole diff, I scoped it to the one transferable thing in it: **`?? 0` on a field that is always missing turns a sort into a tie, and the tie-break silently becomes the ranking.** That's a bug class, not a DG quirk — the fourth quiz question replays it as a task list sorted by `priority ?? 0`, so the shape transfers.

Four retrieval questions with immediate feedback, then the checklist to carry into your next review. Primary source is [Google's "What to look for in a code review"](https://google.github.io/eng-practices/review/reviewer/looking-for.html) — its *Functionality* section makes exactly the distinction this bug turns on: whether the code behaves as the author **intended**, not whether each line is correct.

## Two things worth flagging

**I found defects reviewing my own quiz.** Q2 and Q4 had options with unequal word counts (4 vs 5), which leaks the answer through formatting. Fixed, then validated all four programmatically — uniform word counts, answer keys pointing at the intended option.

**I verified the quiz actually runs** rather than assuming. Served the workspace over HTTP, clicked an answer, and confirmed the right option highlights, feedback appears, options disable, and the score reads `1 of 1 correct (4 total)`. Server's stopped now.

## The learning record

I logged that during ENG-1734 you rejected my `rank`-field fix unprompted and proposed reusing the providers' existing order — which was correct and deleted ~40 lines. That sets the pitch: you're already reasoning about whether a computation should exist, so lessons stay at "name and generalise the failure mode" rather than explaining language mechanics.

Candidates queued in `NOTES.md` for next time: verifying runtime payload shape vs trusting optional types (the `Object.keys()` dump is what actually found this bug); separating defects a PR introduced from pre-existing debt (the review returned 9 findings, only 2 were yours); and rank fusion as the principled answer to incomparable scores.
